What should an Oklahoma City homeowner know before selling?

Oklahoma City is large enough that selling a house depends on which part of it you are in, which county bills the property and which school district the address falls in. A seller can list, sell privately or take a cash offer, and this page walks through the local facts that shape each choice.

How big is Oklahoma City and which counties does it cover?

Oklahoma City covers 620.79 square miles, of which 601.11 is land, and it is the county seat of Oklahoma County. Its limits also reach into Canadian, Cleveland and Pottawatomie counties, though the parts outside Oklahoma County are mostly suburban or rural watershed land. The 2020 census counted 681,054 residents.

Because the city crosses county lines, the tax bill for a house depends on the county where it sits. Most addresses are billed by the Oklahoma County Treasurer, but a house in the southern edge may be billed by Cleveland County. Check the parcel before you plan closing figures.

How is Oklahoma City laid out?

The city is split by the North Canadian River, renamed the Oklahoma River inside city limits in 2004. North and south sides have a different character, according to Wikipedia: the north has urban neighborhoods near the center and sprawling suburbs further out, while the south is more industrial and grew up around the Stockyards and meatpacking plants.

The city also has three large lakes, Hefner and Overholser in the northwest and Stanley Draper in the far southeast. Downtown had about 7,600 residents in the Wikipedia count, and the city lies in the Sandstone Hills with Cross Timbers terrain in the northeast. A buyer for a south side bungalow and a buyer for a north side suburban house are usually different people, so pricing and marketing differ.

What is Oklahoma City's history in brief?

Oklahoma City was founded in the Land Run of 1889 and grew to more than 10,000 people within hours. The April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building killed 168 people.

The oil bust that followed the 1982 Penn Square Bank collapse hit the city's housing market hard, as Wikipedia describes it, and downtown has been rebuilt since through public projects. The point for sellers: Oklahoma City real estate has gone through sharp cycles tied to energy prices, so ask for current local sales data rather than relying on old rules of thumb.

Who are the major employers in Oklahoma City?

The State of Oklahoma is the largest, followed by Tinker Air Force Base. The list below is from Wikipedia's March 2024 table of top employers:

Devon Energy and Expand Energy, both Fortune 500 companies, are headquartered here. Tinker, in the southeast, is described as the largest military air depot in the nation. Job transfers to and from these employers are a common reason for a fast sale, since a move date can be set by an employer, not the housing market.

What does Oklahoma City weather mean for a house?

Severe weather season runs from March through June, especially April and May, and the city has been struck by about 150 tornadoes since 1890 along with hail and occasional derechoes. Wikipedia counts 13 violent tornadoes in the city's record. Annual precipitation is about 35.9 inches and temperatures reach 100 degrees on about 10.4 days a year.

Wikipedia also notes that droughts and flash flooding both occur regularly. A buyer's inspector will concentrate on:

  • Roof age and hail damage
  • Storm shelter or safe room condition
  • Foundation movement after dry spells and heavy rain
  • Drainage and creek or floodplain proximity

The city runs a Storm Shelter Registry where residents can register a shelter's address, type and location to help first responders. Registering a shelter and keeping its permit record is useful documentation at sale.

What code rules can affect an Oklahoma City sale?

Oklahoma City code enforcement acts on complaints. An inspector visits, issues a notice, and enforcement follows if the problem is not fixed by the next visit. For overgrown lots and junk the city can clean up and bill the owner, and for exterior maintenance violations it can write citations.

Common rules sellers should check before listing:

  • Grass is a violation at 12 inches, and owners must maintain adjacent alleys and right-of-way.
  • Vehicles that are inoperable, wrecked or junked are a public nuisance after 72 hours.
  • Parking on an unpaved surface or sidewalk, including boats, trailers and RVs, is a violation.
  • Roofs, fences and painted surfaces must be kept in good repair.
  • Dilapidated and unsecured structures, with damaged foundations or open doors and windows, violate state law as well as city code.
  • Bulk waste may go to the curb no more than three days before pickup.

The county treasurer's office notes that special assessments for weeds, cleaning, paving and nuisance abatement are certified to the treasurer after they become delinquent and are placed as a lien on the property account. That lien can show up in a title search. See the city's code enforcement page.

How do property taxes work for an Oklahoma County home?

The Oklahoma County Assessor sets values and the Treasurer collects the bill. Taxes can be paid in full or in two installments, with the first half or the full amount due by December 31. If nothing is paid by then, the whole amount becomes delinquent on January 1, and if half is paid the rest is due March 31.

Interest on delinquent payments is 18 percent a year, added at 1.5 percent monthly on the 15th, and a missing statement is not a legal reason to waive it. The Treasurer says assessments are certified to its office on October 1, and a new owner should give the assessor a correct mailing address before September 30. Mortgage servicers often pay through a third-party tax service, so a payment can take time to appear online.

When a house sells, the closing agent normally prorates the current year's tax and pays any unpaid balance from the seller's proceeds. Look up your account on the county's public access search before you list.

How do you get around Oklahoma City?

Interstates 35, 40 and 44 pass through the city, with I-235 and I-240 as connectors. The stretch of I-44 between NW 23rd and NW 36th Streets carried about 167,200 vehicles a day in 2018, the busiest road in the state. Will Rogers World Airport served 4,341,159 passengers in 2018, and Amtrak stops at the Santa Fe Depot downtown.

Commute time matters to buyers, so a house near an interstate ramp or the Kilpatrick Turnpike has a different appeal than one far from the highway grid.

Which school districts serve Oklahoma City addresses?

Oklahoma City Public Schools covers the largest part of the city, but many other districts overlap it. In Oklahoma County Wikipedia lists Putnam City, Western Heights, Mid-Del, Moore, Edmond, Deer Creek, Mustang, Harrah, Choctaw/Nicoma Park and others. Districts in Cleveland County covering part of the city include Moore and Little Axe.

A single Oklahoma City mailing address can sit in any of these, so confirm the district from the county records or the school district's boundary tool.

What do Oklahoma City sellers usually run into?

  • Hail or storm damage with an open or denied insurance claim
  • Inherited houses in older neighborhoods where heirs are out of state
  • Rental houses with deferred maintenance or an open code notice
  • Vacant houses that attract weed, junk or unsecured-structure complaints
  • Owners facing a job relocation or a mortgage problem

A cash buyer typically purchases a house in its current condition and covers the closing paperwork the buyer handles. Compare any offer with what a listing would net after repairs, fees and time on the market, and ask for the terms in writing before agreeing.

More questions about Oklahoma City, OK

Is Oklahoma City in more than one county?

Yes. The city is the county seat of Oklahoma County, and its limits extend into Canadian, Cleveland and Pottawatomie counties. The county that bills the house depends on where the parcel sits.

When are Oklahoma County property taxes due?

The first half or the full amount is due by December 31. If nothing is paid by then, the whole amount is delinquent January 1, and if half is paid the rest is due March 31.

What interest rate applies to late property tax in Oklahoma County?

The Treasurer charges 18 percent a year on delinquent payments, added monthly at 1.5 percent on the 15th. Not receiving a statement does not waive the interest.

How high can grass be in Oklahoma City before it is a violation?

City ordinance treats grass as a violation at 12 inches. Owners are also responsible for alleys and right-of-way next to their property, and the city can clean up and bill the owner.

Can I sell an Oklahoma City house with code violations or storm damage?

Yes. Cash buyers purchase houses in their present condition, though open code notices or liens may need to be handled at closing. Get the terms in writing before you decide.

How big is Tulsa and which counties does it cover?

Tulsa is Oklahoma's second-largest city, with 413,066 residents in the 2020 census and a metro area of 1,034,123, according to Wikipedia's census figures. The city spans 201.85 square miles and reaches into four counties: Tulsa, Osage, Rogers and Wagoner.

That four-county reach matters to a seller because the county decides who values and bills your property. Most Tulsa houses are in Tulsa County, but a parcel on the edges can belong to Osage, Rogers or Wagoner County, each with its own assessor and treasurer. Check the county on your tax statement before you call anyone.

School boundaries are just as split. Wikipedia lists Tulsa, Berryhill, Bixby, Broken Arrow, Jenks, Owasso and Union districts for the parts of Tulsa inside Tulsa County, and Tulsa Public Schools for the Osage County part. Tulsa Public Schools has nine high schools and more than 41,000 students per that source, which ranks it the second-largest district in the state.

What are Tulsa's main areas, and how do they differ for sellers?

Tulsa is a set of very different areas, and a house's location changes how it is priced and who buys it. Wikipedia's neighborhood overview describes these:

  • Downtown: about 1.4 square miles inside the Inner Dispersal Loop, with the Oil Capital Historic District, Blue Dome, Tulsa Arts District and Greenwood. Surrounding areas include Owen Park, The Pearl, The Heights and Kendall-Whittier.
  • Midtown: the historic residential core, with early 20th-century homes in art deco to Greek Revival styles in Maple Ridge, Swan Lake, Cherry Street, Brookside and Lortondale.
  • South Tulsa: mostly developed since the 1970s, with lower-density suburban housing and retail.
  • East of Highway 169: a diverse area with much of the city's manufacturing.
  • West Tulsa: west of the Arkansas River, with large parks, reserves and oil refineries.

A century-old Midtown house and a 1980s south Tulsa ranch face different inspection issues. The older house tends to draw questions on wiring, plumbing and foundations. The newer one draws questions on roof age and heating and cooling.

What is Tulsa's economy built on?

Energy first, then a broader base. The United States Oil and Gas Association was founded in Tulsa in 1917, and the city is again home to the headquarters of firms such as Williams Companies, ONE Gas, ONEOK and Helmerich and Payne, per Wikipedia.

The same source says Tulsa manufacturers account for about 60 percent of Oklahoma's exports, small businesses make up more than 80 percent of city companies, and 30 companies employ over 1,000 people locally. Those are older figures, so use them for scale rather than a current count.

Aviation also matters: Tulsa International Airport serves more than three million travelers a year, and the Port of Catoosa moves goods by water. For sellers, a job change at one of these employers is a common reason a family has to move on a deadline.

Does Tulsa weather affect a house sale?

It does. Tulsa has a humid subtropical climate, an average temperature of 61.3 degrees and just under 41 inches of precipitation a year, with May the wettest month at 5.9 inches. Spring and early summer bring severe thunderstorms with large hail, damaging winds and sometimes tornadoes.

Flooding has shaped the city's rules. After a stalled front dropped 15 inches of rain overnight in 1984, killing 14 people and destroying 7,000 buildings, Tulsa built what Wikipedia calls one of the nation's most extensive flood control systems, and FEMA honored it for floodplain management in the early 1990s and again in 2000.

If your house sits near a creek or in a mapped flood area, expect the buyer's lender to ask about flood insurance. Triple-digit heat averages 11 days a year, which puts air conditioning on the inspection list as well.

How does Tulsa code enforcement work, and what happens if you ignore a notice?

Tulsa's Code Enforcement handles nuisance, zoning and property maintenance rules for occupied, commercial and vacant properties, and investigates about 22,000 violations across more than 18,000 cases a year, per the city. Reports go to 311 or tulsa311.com.

StepWhat the city says
Priority 1Unsecured structures, vehicles on blocks, blocked sidewalks, raw sewage
Priority 3Tall grass, trash, junk and debris, handled in order received
NoticeOwner gets 10 days to comply
ExtensionsUp to two 10-day extensions at $64 each, not available for every violation
AbatementIf the city does the work, the owner pays the cost plus a $300 processing fee

The city's "Up to Code" brochure adds that grass over 12 inches, unsecured vacant structures and inoperable vehicles stored outdoors are violations. An owner must board up a vacant structure after a fire, and openings broken in a break-in must be secured immediately.

Anyone can search a property's code cases back to 2018 through the city's self-service portal. Buyers can do the same, so assume they will see an open case on your address. Clearing it before you list avoids a surprise at the table.

How does property tax work for a Tulsa County house?

In Tulsa County, the Assessor sets the value as of January 1 and the Treasurer collects the bill. The Assessor's important dates page lists the following:

  • January 1 to March 15: apply for most exemptions, including homestead. Late applications generally wait until the next year.
  • First Monday in April: last day for an informal appeal if you were not mailed an increase notice.
  • May 31: the Board of Equalization adjourns unless it extends to June 30.
  • September 15 to October 1: owner and address updates pause while the tax roll is prepared.
  • October and November: the roll goes to the Treasurer, who mails bills.

The Treasurer's page says at least half the tax must be paid before January 1, and if you pay in halves, the second must be paid before April 1. Because ownership changes are paused each fall, a seller who closes in that window should confirm that the bill still goes to the right person. Title companies normally prorate the tax between buyer and seller.

Remember that Osage, Rogers and Wagoner County parcels follow their own offices and calendars, which we did not verify here.

What are the ways to sell a house in Tulsa?

The three main routes are an agent listing, a sale by owner and a cash offer. Tulsa's large size and many neighborhoods make local pricing matter more than a citywide average.

  • Agent listing: reaches the most buyers, with prep, showings and a financed buyer's appraisal to get through.
  • By owner: avoids a commission but puts pricing and paperwork on you.
  • Cash offer: built for houses with repairs, open code cases, tenants, hail damage or an estate to settle.

Before you decide, pull your code case history, your county tax statement and any storm or insurance claim records. They are the three documents that most often shape how a buyer prices a Tulsa house.

More questions about Tulsa, OK

Is Tulsa only in Tulsa County?

No. The city reaches into Tulsa, Osage, Rogers and Wagoner Counties. Your tax statement shows which county's assessor and treasurer serve your address.

How do I report or look up a code violation in Tulsa?

Call 311 or use tulsa311.com to report one. The city's self-service portal lets you search code cases by address, with results going back to 2018.

How long do I have to fix a Tulsa code violation?

The city's notice gives the owner 10 days to comply. You can buy up to two 10-day extensions at $64 each, though some violations, such as unsecured structures, are not eligible.

When must I file for the homestead exemption in Tulsa County?

The Tulsa County Assessor accepts applications all year, but to count for the current year the application must be filed by March 15 or within 30 days of a valuation-increase notice.

Does hail damage stop me from selling a Tulsa house?

No. You can repair the roof and list the house, or sell it as is to a buyer who accounts for the damage. Keep photos, estimates and any insurance paperwork handy.

Norman is a university city of roughly 131,000 people where the sale of a house is shaped by three things: the University of Oklahoma, the city's large footprint, and Cleveland County's tax and recording offices. A seller here can list the house, sell it privately, or take a cash offer, and each route works differently depending on the condition of the property and how soon the money is needed.

This page covers the city first and then the local steps that tend to matter at closing.

How big is Norman and where does it sit?

Norman is a large, spread-out city. The 2010 figures show 189.42 square miles of total area, 178.77 of them land, and the city center is about 20 miles from the center of Oklahoma City, with Moore lying between the two.

The land changes from west to east. The western side is prairie, while the east around Lake Thunderbird holds roughly 6,000 acres of lakes and Cross Timbers forest. Elevation is close to 1,171 feet. A house on the west side and a house near the lake can have very different yards, drainage and tree cover, even though both carry a Norman address.

How did Norman start?

Norman was founded in the Land Run of April 22, 1889, and incorporated on May 13, 1891. The name comes from Abner Ernest Norman, a 23-year-old surveyor whose crew carved "Norman's Camp" on an elm tree near what is now Classen Boulevard and Lindsey Street.

Two local businessmen lobbied the territorial government for a university, and on December 19, 1890 the council passed the bill that created the University of Oklahoma in Norman, about 17 years before statehood. The completion of Interstate 35 in June 1959 turned Norman into a commuter city for Oklahoma City: the population was 33,412 in 1960 and 52,117 ten years later.

What are Norman's neighborhoods like?

Norman has several well-defined areas, and the right buyer pool differs for each. Wikipedia's neighborhood notes describe a few of them:

  • Downtown, about 2 square miles bounded by University Boulevard, Symmes Street, Porter Avenue and Daws Street, with some of the oldest buildings in Oklahoma.
  • Hall Park, northeast of downtown, annexed in 2005 and advertised in the early 1960s as the first "all-electric town" in the United States.
  • The campus area, with neo-Gothic and Queen Anne style houses and churches.
  • The Miller Historic District and the Chautauqua Historic District, both city-designated preservation districts.

If your house is in a historic district, ask the city's planning staff before doing exterior work, since preservation rules can apply to windows, siding and additions.

Who employs people in Norman, and how does that touch a home sale?

The University of Oklahoma is the largest employer by a wide margin. Norman's 2022 annual financial report, as reproduced on Wikipedia, lists the top employers this way:

Enrollment at the university is about 30,000, per the same article. A school calendar affects timing: houses near campus may turn over around the academic year, and landlords who own rentals near campus may want a sale that does not depend on a tenant's lease end date. The National Weather Center, which houses NOAA and university weather research, is also a significant employer in town.

What is Norman's weather and what does it do to a house?

Norman has a humid subtropical climate with average annual precipitation near 38 inches. May and June are the wettest months, and July daytime highs average about 92.5 degrees Fahrenheit.

Tornado season peaks from March through June. Wikipedia notes a high-end EF2 tornado on the southeast side of the city on the night of February 26, 2023, and tornado events in Cleveland County on May 10, 2010 that destroyed homes and businesses inside the city limits. A buyer's inspector will pay attention to roof age, hail damage and any storm shelter. Keep repair receipts and insurance paperwork ready.

How do I get around Norman and the metro?

Norman is a car-based city. About 80 percent of residents drive alone to work, per the Wikipedia figure, and Interstate 35 carried more than 99,000 vehicles a day in 2007. State Highway 9 and U.S. 77 are the other main routes.

Embark provides fare-free bus and paratransit service across the Norman area, with express service to downtown Oklahoma City. Amtrak's Heartland Flyer stops at the Norman Depot with daily round trips to Oklahoma City and Fort Worth. Will Rogers World Airport is about 20 miles northwest. These details help in a listing description and in answering a buyer's commute questions.

What permits and codes apply in Norman?

Norman adopted updated building, fire and property maintenance codes effective June 22, 2023. The list includes the 2018 International Building, Residential, Existing Building, Plumbing and Property Maintenance codes, the 2018 Fuel Gas Code and the 2020 National Electrical Code, with state and local amendments.

Permits and inspections are handled by the Development Services Division at 225 N. Webster Avenue. Its checklist for one and two family construction includes new homes, additions, alterations, storm shelters and storage buildings, so a garage shelter or backyard shed may have a permit file. Reviewing that record before listing can prevent a surprise from a buyer's lender. The city's building codes page lists the adopted codes.

What Oklahoma transfer tax applies when a Norman house sells?

Oklahoma charges a documentary stamp tax on deeds. The rate is 75 cents for each $500 of the price or any part of $500, and the tax applies when the price exceeds $100.

At that rate a $200,000 sale needs 400 units of $0.75, or $300 in stamps. The county clerk sells and affixes the stamps when the deed is filed, and the Oklahoma Tax Commission says either side of the deed can be held responsible, so the contract should say who pays. Deeds between related people without payment and deeds to a person's own revocable trust are among the listed exemptions in 68 O.S. section 3202.

On the property tax side, Cleveland County says half the bill is due by December 31 and the second half by March 31.

Which school districts cover Norman?

Norman Public Schools is the largest, with 15 elementary schools, four middle schools and two high schools and more than 17,000 students, per Wikipedia. Noble Public Schools serves southeastern parts of Norman and Little Axe serves the east, while parts of the city fall in McLoud, Mid-Del, Moore and Robin Hill districts.

Because several districts overlap the city, the district for a given address should be confirmed rather than assumed.

What do Norman sellers usually run into?

  • Older homes near campus with outdated wiring or plumbing

A cash buyer will usually look at the house as it stands, which lets the seller skip repairs and showings. Get the offer in writing, ask what the buyer pays for, and compare it with a listed sale after fees and carrying costs.

Oklahoma charges 75 cents for each $500 of the sale price or fraction of it. On a $200,000 sale that comes to $300. The county clerk affixes the stamps when the deed is recorded.

When are Cleveland County property taxes due?

Taxes may be paid in full or in two halves. At least half must be paid by December 31, and the second half is due by March 31, according to Cleveland County.

Which building codes does Norman use?

The city adopted its 2018 International Codes and the 2020 National Electrical Code with local amendments, effective June 22, 2023. Permits and inspections are handled by Development Services at 225 N. Webster Avenue.

Does the University of Oklahoma affect selling a house in Norman?

It can. The university employs about 11,085 people by the city's 2022 report and enrolls roughly 30,000 students, so demand and rental turnover near campus follow the academic calendar.

How big is Broken Arrow and where does it sit?

Broken Arrow covers about 45 square miles in the northeast corner of Oklahoma, in the region known as Green Country, and the 2020 census counted 113,540 residents. That made it the fourth most populous city in the state and a major part of the Tulsa metropolitan area, which had 1,023,988 residents.

Most of the city is in Tulsa County, and areas that extend into Wagoner County are zoned to Broken Arrow Public Schools. The size matters for sellers: a house near the downtown Main Street area, one by the Creek Turnpike on the south side and one on the Wagoner County edge sit in different pockets with different commutes and different county offices.

Green Country is described as the most topographically diverse part of Oklahoma, with hills and lakes, so lots can slope or sit near creeks more than the flat plains image suggests.

What is the history behind the Broken Arrow name?

The name comes from a Creek community in Alabama. After removal along the Trail of Tears in the 1830s, Creek families founded a new settlement in Indian Territory and kept the name, which is Rekackv in the Muscogee language and means broken arrow.

The present townsite dates to 1902, when the Missouri-Kansas-Texas Railroad was granted townsite rights and William S. Fears of the Arkansas Valley Town Site Company chose the location about 18 miles southeast of Tulsa. The line was finished in 1903 and still runs through the middle of the city, now owned by Union Pacific for freight.

Farming and strip coal mining drove the early economy. The city stayed small until the 1960s, when the Broken Arrow Expressway, State Highway 51, linked it to downtown Tulsa. Population went from a little above 11,000 in 1970 to more than 50,000 in 1990 and over 74,000 by 2000. That timeline explains why so much of the housing stock dates from the 1970s onward.

What do Broken Arrow employers and colleges add to the housing market?

Broken Arrow has the third-largest concentration of manufacturers in Oklahoma, even though it grew as a bedroom community for Tulsa workers. City leaders have pushed for more local jobs and shopping so residents spend less time commuting elsewhere.

Education institutions also anchor the area:

  • Northeastern State University's Broken Arrow campus, opened in 2001, with about 3,000 upperclass and graduate students.
  • Tulsa Technology Center's Broken Arrow campus, established in 1983, with about 3,500 secondary and adult students.
  • Rhema Bible Training Center, founded in 1974 on 110 acres.

A house that needs updates can be hard to sell on the open market, since retail buyers often ask for repairs before closing.

Which school districts serve Broken Arrow addresses?

The Tulsa County Assessor values each Broken Arrow property as of January 1 and revalues residential property every year. The valuation notice gives you 30 calendar days to protest in writing, and an informal protest can happen by phone.

Assessed value is 11 percent of taxable fair cash value. Taxable value is capped at a 5 percent yearly rise, or 3 percent with a homestead, but the cap is removed when the property is purchased. A new owner therefore sees a bigger bill than the previous one, which the assessor lists among its common questions.

Homestead applications are due by March 15 or within 30 days of the increase notice to count for the current year. The assessor also notes you owe the whole year's bill on a property as it stood on January 1, even if you sell part of it later.

Older sections of town carry names that sellers will recognize from listings and tax bills, including Kenwood, Waverley, Weatherly, East Hill, Kinser Heights, Buena Vista, McKinley, Southern Heights and East Park.

What is Enid's history, and why does it matter for older houses?

Heavy rain is part of the record too: Enid holds Oklahoma's greatest one-day rainfall total from an official gauge, 15.68 inches on October 11, 1973. Roofs, gutters and foundations are where a buyer's inspector will look first.

Garfield County mails tax bills in November. You can pay in halves: half by December 31 and the rest by March 31, and if nothing is paid by December 31 the full amount becomes delinquent on January 1.

The assessor values property as of January 1 at fair cash value and applies a 12.5 percent ratio. As its own example, a $100,000 home with a $102.02 millage rate and the homestead exemption comes to about $1,173 in tax. Homestead applications are due by March 15 for the current year. The assessor sends change of valuation notices in the first week of March and the protest period ends on the first Monday in April, or 30 days from the date on a valuation notice.

The Garfield County Treasurer (580-237-0246) handles payment and tax roll searches. At closing, the title company normally checks the treasurer's records and settles any unpaid balance, so it is worth looking up your parcel before you list.

An Oklahoma seller must give the buyer either a property disclaimer statement or a property condition disclosure statement. If you list the house, disclosures, repairs requested after inspection and agent commissions all shape what you keep. If you sell to a company that buys houses for cash, the sale usually goes by contract between you and the buyer, and the disclosure still applies.

Enid's older housing stock and its mix of military and agricultural households mean timing varies a lot between owners. If a lender is already involved, ask for a payoff figure first. Utilities are unusual. Stillwater has had a community-owned electric utility since 1907, and the Stillwater Utilities Authority now provides electric, water, wastewater and solid waste service.   • Additional homestead: another $1,000 for qualifying homeowners with household income of $30,000 or less
  • Senior valuation limitation: caps increases in fair cash value for a head of household age 65 or older who meets the income limit, without freezing the bill
  • Disabled veteran and surviving spouse exemptions, and the storm shelter exemption

For disputes, the Oklahoma Tax Commission's informal protest form says a taxpayer has 30 calendar days from the date the valuation notice was mailed to file a written complaint with the assessor. The first train reached the new depot on November 1, 1899, and the post office was renamed Owasso on January 24, 1900. The name comes from an Osage word that Wikipedia glosses as "the end of the trail," a nod to the turnaround Y where the rail line stopped.

The town plat was signed on March 26, 1904, the town was incorporated that year, and Owasso was chartered as a city in 1972. Until a water tower went up in 1924, water was hauled in by barrel from Owasso Lake.

For a seller the practical point is that the older streets near the original townsite and the newer tracts on the edges behave differently when a buyer's inspector walks through. Older homes tend to prompt questions about wiring, plumbing and foundations, and newer ones about roofs and storm damage.

Which counties and school district cover an Owasso address?

Owasso Public Schools covers 72 square miles, including territory in both Tulsa County and Rogers County, so the county that bills your property tax depends on where the parcel sits. The district says it is one of the largest in Oklahoma.

The district reports enrollment of about 9,100 on its new-family page, served by 15 instructional sites. Its home page shows a higher round figure of 9,700, so the number moves depending on the date and the page you read. The structure is the same either way:

  • Nine elementary schools, including Ator, Bailey, Barnes, Hodson, Mills, Morrow, Northeast, Smith and Stone Canyon
  • Separate 6th, 7th and 8th Grade Centers
  • Owasso High School, split into a West Campus for grades 9 and 10 and an East Campus for grades 11 and 12
  • Ram Academy for grades 9 to 12

The district offers an address lookup map so a buyer can check which school and bus stop a house is tied to. Sellers can mention that link in a listing or when talking to a buyer. It saves a round of questions.

What drives Owasso's economy and the local housing demand?

Owasso's economic development office says the area's major employers keep more than 12,000 workers on the payroll, naming American Airlines, Verizon, Whirlpool, Nordam, Honeywell and Macy's. The city says the large daytime workforce supports local retailers and restaurants, and the same workforce needs housing nearby.

The city has also identified target industries it wants to grow. They are listed on the city's economic development site:

  • Aircraft parts manufacturing, tied to Cherokee Industrial Park and the regional aviation cluster
  • Medical services and research, anchored by Bailey Medical Center and Ascension St. John
  • Film and television, including a 27,000-square-foot Cherokee Film soundstage off Highway 20
  • Metal manufacturing, offices and headquarters, and information technology, with office growth in the Redbud District and along U.S. 169

The same page says more than 64.8 percent of working residents are in managerial, financial, professional, administrative or sales fields, compared with 58.2 percent statewide. Owasso also sits on the South Kansas and Oklahoma Railroad, which links to Tulsa and the Port of Catoosa. A seller whose job moved, or whose employer did, is a common reason for a quick sale in a commuter city like this.

Does Owasso weather affect what a buyer will ask about the house?

Yes. Owasso sits in Tornado Alley with a humid subtropical climate, an average yearly temperature near 60 degrees Fahrenheit and about 39.5 inches of precipitation, per Wikipedia's climate summary.

Buyers and their inspectors in this region look hard at the roof, gutters, windows and any storm shelter. Payne County's assessor page notes that Oklahoma exempts up to 100 square feet of a qualifying tornado shelter or safe room installed after January 1, 2002 from property tax, so a house with a shelter has a documented selling point. Have the paperwork ready.

If storm damage is unrepaired, say so up front. A cash buyer prices the roof as it is, while a retail buyer using a loan may need repairs finished before an appraiser will sign off.

What does the City of Owasso require before you repair or change a house?

Owasso requires a building permit for many projects, and the Community Development office publishes plain answers. Missing permits are one of the most common surprises when an owner decides to sell.

Two items matter most for sellers. A converted garage with no permit can stall a financed sale. And the city does not license contractors, so any contractor you hire must hold a state license. The inspection line is 918-376-1542, and same-day inspections need a request in before 2 p.m., per the city's FAQ.

The zoning verification letter is worth knowing about if you are selling a house with a workshop, a rental room or an odd addition. The city will list open violations and certificates of occupancy if you ask.

How does property tax work for an Owasso seller?

For a home in the Tulsa County part of Owasso, the Tulsa County Assessor sets the value and the County Treasurer bills and collects the tax. The Assessor's calendar says homestead applications are accepted all year but must be filed by March 15, or within 30 days of a valuation-increase notice, to count for the current year.

Other dates on that calendar:

  • First Monday in April: last day for an informal appeal if no increase notice was mailed
  • May 31: the county Board of Equalization adjourns unless it votes to extend to June 30
  • September 15 to October 1: owner and address changes are suspended while the tax roll is built
  • October: the roll goes to the Treasurer; November: bills are mailed

The Treasurer's page says at least half the tax is due before January 1 and the second half before April 1. If you sell between those dates, the closing agent normally prorates the bill. Ask the title company for the proration line early. Parcels on the Rogers County side of the district are handled by that county's offices, and we did not verify its calendar, so check with them directly.

What are the ways to sell a house in Owasso?

You can list with an agent, sell on your own, or take a cash offer from a buyer who buys as-is. The right pick depends on repairs, timing and how much you want to manage.

  • Listing with an agent: usually the widest market, but you prepare the house, allow showings and wait on a buyer's loan and appraisal.
  • Selling yourself: you keep the commission but handle pricing, disclosures, contracts and negotiation.
  • Cash offer: fewer steps and a closing date you can choose, with the offer reflecting the house in its current condition.

On the deed side, Oklahoma charges a documentary stamp tax of 75 cents for each $500 of the price, with liens left out of the base, per the notice posted by the Payne County Clerk. The buyer's full address must appear on the deed, and any claimed exemption has to be written on its face with the statute cited. Your title company handles this, but it helps to know it exists.

What do Owasso sellers usually run into?

Most of the situations we see in a suburb like Owasso involve timing and condition rather than a lack of buyers. Common ones include a relocation for work, an inherited house that nobody wants to maintain, a tenant who has moved out and left damage, or a roof the owner cannot afford to replace.

Write down the items an inspector is likely to flag, gather any permits for past work, and check the school and county for your address. With those facts on paper you can compare a listing, a private sale and a cash offer on equal terms, and decide without pressure.

More questions about Owasso, OK

Is Owasso in Tulsa County or Rogers County?

Mostly Tulsa County, though Owasso Public Schools covers territory in both Tulsa and Rogers Counties. Check your property record to see which county's assessor and treasurer handle your parcel.

Do I need a permit before I sell an Owasso house with a converted garage?

The city requires a building permit with plans to enclose a garage. If the work was done without one, talk to Community Development at 918-376-1540 before listing, because an unpermitted conversion can slow a financed buyer.

When are property taxes due on a house in the Tulsa County part of Owasso?

The Tulsa County Treasurer says at least half is due before January 1 and the rest before April 1. Bills are mailed in November, per the Assessor's calendar.

How can I check which school my Owasso house is zoned for?

Owasso Public Schools posts an interactive map where you enter the address to see the assigned schools and bus stop. The Enrollment Center at 918-274-1904 can confirm boundaries.

How long does a cash sale take compared with listing?

A cash sale can close on a date you choose once the title work is done, because no lender appraisal is involved. A listed sale depends on showings, the buyer's loan and the appraisal, so it varies more.

Where is Bartlesville and what shapes the housing here?

Bartlesville sits in Washington County in northeastern Oklahoma, with a small part of the city extending into Osage County. The Caney River runs through town and separates downtown from the east side.

The 2020 census counted 37,290 residents and 17,140 housing units, and 11.7% of those units were vacant. Among occupied homes, 66.3% were owner-occupied and 33.7% were rented. For a seller, that mix means a fair number of buyers are investors or landlords as well as owner-occupants.

The city covers about 21 square miles and is largely built out. The town was incorporated in 1897 and platted in 1898, so many of the older neighborhoods around downtown carry houses that are a century old or close to it. Those homes often come with original plumbing, wiring and foundations that a buyer's inspector will look at closely.

What is Bartlesville's economy built on?

Oil built Bartlesville, and energy companies still anchor the job market. Oklahoma's first commercial oil well, the Nellie Johnstone No. 1, came in along the Caney River on April 15, 1897, and Frank and L.E. Phillips founded Phillips Petroleum here in 1917.

Phillips Petroleum later merged into ConocoPhillips, and the company spun off Phillips 66 in 2012. The two companies together employ or contract with more than 3,800 people in the area,, and Chevron Phillips also keeps an office in town.

Other employers and institutions shape demand for housing too:

  • Two industrial parks, the Bartlesville Industrial Park and the Sunset Industrial Park, where a lithium-ion battery recycling plant landed in September 2023.
  • Oklahoma Wesleyan University, with about 1,100 students, and a Rogers State University branch campus downtown with about 700.
  • Tri County Technology Center, which runs career training for high school and adult students.

What does Bartlesville weather mean for a house?

Bartlesville has a humid subtropical climate with hot summers, cool winters and most of its rain in spring. It sits in Tornado Alley, so severe weather is most common from April through June.

That swing from triple digits to deep cold is hard on roofs, HVAC equipment and exposed plumbing. A buyer who sees stained ceilings, a patched roof or an old furnace will price the repair in, and a cash buyer usually does the same arithmetic before making an offer.

How have floods and tornadoes affected Bartlesville properties?

Two floods and one major tornado are part of the city's recent record, and each can show up in buyer questions. The Caney River flooded in October 1986 after unusually heavy rain, splitting the city in half for several days. It broke its banks again in June 2007 and crested five feet below the 1986 level.

An EF4 tornado struck Bartlesville and nearby Barnsdall on May 6, 2024, and debris cleanup was still under way in July 2024. Buyers often ask whether storm repairs were permitted and finished.

The city also warns that some properties lie in floodplains or floodways. Development there can be regulated or prohibited, and a floodplain development permit may be required before you add to or alter a structure. If your house is near the river, expect a buyer to ask about flood zone status and insurance before they sign.

Which Bartlesville city rules matter before you sell?

The city's Building and Construction Services division handles permits, and its page advises calling 918.338.4244 before any project to confirm whether a permit applies. Unpermitted work is a common source of delays at closing, so it is worth checking before you list or accept an offer.

According to the division, permits are required for:

  • Structural construction, alteration, demolition or remodel, including re-roofing that changes the roof structure.
  • Fences over seven feet and walls over four feet.
  • Electrical work, including solar and generator installs.
  • Mechanical work such as furnaces, water heaters and fuel-gas piping.
  • Plumbing, with limited exceptions for faucet repairs and clearing stoppages.
  • Pools or hot tubs 24 inches or deeper.

Painting, tile, carpet, cabinets and like-for-like replacement of doors and windows do not need a building permit. The city enforces the state's minimum construction codes, adopted by the Oklahoma Uniform Building Code Commission.

How does Bartlesville enforce property maintenance?

The Neighborhood Services Division enforces the city's minimum property maintenance codes and typically acts on complaints rather than patrolling. Its page lists the most common violations as tall grass and weeds, junk and trash, deteriorated fences and structures, broken windows, parking on grass, inoperable vehicles, improperly stored recreational vehicles and illegal signs.

The division reports that more than 2,000 complaints are filed and investigated in a year, and about 97 percent are resolved through voluntary compliance. Complaints can be filed online, at City Hall, 401 S. Johnstone Ave., or by phone at 918.338.4230.

Owners of vacant or deteriorated buildings should know about the Voluntary Demolition Program. It lets owners demolish dilapidated structures at a reduced fee and avoid nuisance actions, though participation is voluntary and funding is limited. A neglected inherited house with open code complaints is a typical reason owners here look at a direct sale.

How does property tax work for a Bartlesville home in Washington County?

The Washington County Assessor values every property as of January 1 each year, and the county treasurer bills the tax. The assessor's office says it runs a four-year revaluation cycle, so each property is visually inspected at least once in that period.

If you disagree with the value, start with an informal protest by visiting the assessor, who arranges a follow-up inspection. You can then file a written protest with the county Board of Equalization, an independent three-member board. If that fails, you may appeal to district court within twenty days after the Board adjourns or twenty days after May 31, whichever is later.

The county says the assessor sets value, not the tax rate. Schools, cities and townships set levies after public hearings. Contact the assessor at (918) 337-2830 or the treasurer at 918-337-2810. Homestead status matters when you sell: the assessor asks owners to report it if they sell or stop living in the house as their primary residence.

What paperwork does an Oklahoma seller in Bartlesville handle at closing?

Oklahoma charges a documentary stamp tax on deeds at 75 cents for each $500 of consideration, collected by the county clerk when the deed is recorded. On a $150,000 sale, that is 300 units of $500, or $225.

The statute says the tax is paid by anyone who makes, signs, issues or sells the instrument, and the Oklahoma Tax Commission notes both grantor and grantee can be held responsible. Your purchase contract decides who pays in practice, and the Washington County Clerk records the deed.

Oklahoma law also requires sellers of one or two residential units to give the buyer either a property condition disclosure statement or a disclaimer statement under 60 O.S. section 833. Sellers who choose a disclosure should fill it out honestly, because the form covers roof, plumbing, electrical and other systems.

Which schools and roads serve Bartlesville?

Almost all of the Washington County part of Bartlesville falls in Bartlesville Public Schools, Independent School District 30, which runs six elementary sites, Central and Madison middle schools and the high school. A few northern parts fall in Dewey Public Schools, and some Osage County sections are covered by Dewey and Osage Hills.

US-75 runs north and south, US-60 runs east and west, and State Highway 123 also serves the city. Tulsa International Airport is about 45 miles south, and Bartlesville Municipal Airport, a city-owned single-runway field, handles general aviation. Buyers commuting to Tulsa often ask about drive time, so mention it in any listing or offer conversation.

More questions about Bartlesville, OK

Can I sell a house in Bartlesville with code violations?

Yes. Open code complaints do not prevent a sale, but they must be dealt with or disclosed, and a buyer will price them in. Contact Neighborhood Services at 918.338.4230 to learn what is open on your property.

Do I need a permit to repair a roof in Bartlesville?

It depends on the work. The city says re-roofing that changes the roof structure or framework needs a building permit, and the division suggests calling 918.338.4244 to confirm before starting.

Does Washington County send a notice when my home value changes?

Oklahoma assessors value property as of January 1 each year. The county describes an informal protest, then a Board of Equalization appeal, then district court, so keep any valuation notice and call (918) 337-2830 promptly with questions.

Is Bartlesville in a flood zone?

Parts of it are. The city notes some properties lie in floodplains or floodways, and the Caney River flooded the city in 1986 and 2007. Check your parcel with the city's engineering department before you list.

What does a documentary stamp tax cost on a Bartlesville sale?

The rate is 75 cents per $500 of consideration. A $200,000 price works out to 400 units, or $300, paid when the deed is recorded with the county clerk.

What should a Muskogee homeowner know before selling?

Selling a house in Muskogee means dealing with a smaller city that has a long industrial history, a strict nuisance-abatement process and an unusual tax question that came up in 2026. Owners can list, sell privately or take a cash offer, and in Muskogee the condition of the house and the city's code rules often decide which route makes sense.

This page covers the city, its economy and weather, the local code and tax issues, and the steps at closing.

Where is Muskogee and what is its geography?

Muskogee is the county seat of Muskogee County in eastern Oklahoma, about 50 miles southeast of Tulsa. The Census Bureau lists 44.5 square miles of total area, of which 43.0 is land.

The Arkansas, Verdigris and Grand rivers meet in the northeast corner of the city, an area historically called Three Rivers. Elevation is low for Oklahoma, around 600 feet, and the city sits on the line between the eastern oak and hickory forest and the prairie of the Great Plains. Low ground and river valleys are worth checking on a flood map before a house goes on the market.

How did Muskogee grow?

The first permanent settlement near Muskogee dates to 1817 on the south bank of the Verdigris River. After the Indian Removal Act of 1830 the Muscogee (Creek) Nation was relocated here, and the Indian Agency building on Agency Hill, now inside Honor Heights Park, hosted meetings of the Five Civilized Tribes.

The Missouri, Kansas and Texas Railroad reached the area in 1872, a federal court opened in Muskogee in 1889, and the city incorporated in 1898. Businessman Charles N. Haskell, who later became Oklahoma's first governor, moved in during 1901 and helped build railroads and a five-story business block. Muskogee's population passed 25,000 by 1910. In 1905 delegates met here to draft a constitution for a proposed State of Sequoyah, which was never authorized.

What is Muskogee's economy based on?

Muskogee is an economic center for eastern Oklahoma with a manufacturing base. Georgia-Pacific operates a tissue and paper towel plant of 2.9 million square feet, listed as the city's largest employer with about 800 workers.

Two newer announcements are worth watching:

  • Stardust Power broke ground on January 22, 2025 for a lithium refinery near the Port of Muskogee, described as a $1.2 billion project with an initial capacity of 25,000 metric tons a year.
  • On November 20, 2025 Google announced two data centers in the Muskogee area, one near Summit about 7 miles south and one near Council Hill about 25 miles southeast.

The Port of Muskogee sits on the McClellan-Kerr Arkansas River Navigation System, and Union Pacific and BNSF serve the city by rail. Higher education includes Northeastern State University, Connors State College and Indian Capital Technology Center. The effect on housing demand is not something we can promise, so treat these projects as context, not a forecast.

How does Muskogee code enforcement affect a house sale?

Muskogee Code Enforcement responds to complaints about nuisance, zoning and property maintenance violations. The most common are high weeds and grass, trash and debris, vehicles parked on the grass, people living in an RV outside an RV park, inoperable vehicles and derelict structures.

The city says complaints are anonymous and that the legal process takes time, asking residents to allow 15 to 20 business days for results. The number is (918) 684-6235. Sellers of vacant or neglected houses should clear yard violations before showings, because an open notice can come up in a buyer's search of city records.

The city's code of ordinances also states that vacant, abandoned or dilapidated structures create blight and lower property values. A house in that condition may be a candidate for condemnation, so heirs and out-of-town owners should check their status early. You can read the city's code enforcement page for current details.

What is the $29.25 million judgment issue and how could it affect property taxes?

In a September 1, 2026 letter, City Manager Kendal Francis said three inverse condemnation cases against the city, filed in 2007, resulted in judgments totaling $29.25 million plus interest. The cases were England ($8.5 million), Taff ($6.5 million) and Lacey ($14.25 million), and they arose from properties condemned and demolished under the city's nuisance abatement process about twenty years ago. The council approved settlement agreements on August 24, 2026.

The letter explains that Oklahoma cities use a sinking fund, paid by property tax, to cover court judgments. If the full amount were placed on it, the impact would be roughly $450 a year per $100,000 of property valuation, based on information from the Muskogee County Assessor. The decision would not need to be made until June 2027, any increase would begin in October 2027, and it would stay on the tax rolls for three years. The council said it is exploring other ways to pay.

No final decision had been announced in that letter, so sellers should treat this as a possibility, not a set bill. A buyer comparing taxes may ask about it, and the letter is public on the city website.

How are Muskogee property taxes calculated?

The Muskogee County Assessor explains the formula in a one-page guide. The assessor sets fair cash value, the Oklahoma constitution requires real property to be assessed at no less than 11 percent and no more than 13.5 percent of that value, and the result is multiplied by the millage rate of the taxing districts.

The guide's worked example uses a $300,000 house: $300,000 times 11 percent is $33,000, and at 102.39 mills the bill is $3,379. It says about 24 school districts operate in the county, with rates ranging from 76.22 mills in Wainwright to 105.49 in Hilldale, which works out to $2,515 versus $3,481 on the same example. Hilldale Public Schools covers a small southern part of Muskogee, so where a house sits can change the bill.

As in the rest of Oklahoma, county information says tax is payable in two halves, with the first half due by December 31 and the second by March 31, so a closing in early year usually involves a tax proration or a payoff from the seller's proceeds.

Which schools serve Muskogee, and how do you get around?

Muskogee Public Schools covers most of the city limits and a large part of the county. Hilldale Public Schools serves a small southern portion and Fort Gibson Public Schools includes some areas in the east.

Roads include U.S. 62, 64 and 69 and State Highways 16 and 165, plus the Muskogee Turnpike. Davis Regional Airport is five miles south of downtown and has a 7,202-foot runway, while commercial flights use Tulsa International about 49 miles northwest.

What is the weather in Muskogee?

Muskogee is warmer and more humid than much of Oklahoma. The record high is 118 degrees Fahrenheit, set August 10, 1936, and the record low is minus 14 on February 13, 1905. Average annual precipitation in the 1991 to 2020 normals is about 43 inches, with May the wettest month at 5.25 inches.

Heat, humidity and rain are hard on roofs, crawl spaces and older siding, so buyers often ask about moisture history. A recent roof or documented drainage fix helps a listing or a cash conversation.

What do Muskogee sellers usually run into?

  • Vacant or inherited houses with overgrown lots or open code notices
  • Older homes that need roof, foundation or plumbing work
  • Rental properties where tenants have left the property in poor condition
  • Owners worried about the possible tax increase
  • Sellers who live out of town and cannot manage repairs

A cash buyer will usually buy a house as it is, including those with code issues, but the price will reflect repairs and risk. Ask for the offer in writing and compare it with the net from a repaired and listed sale.

More questions about Muskogee, OK

How long does Muskogee code enforcement take to resolve a complaint?

The city asks residents to allow 15 to 20 business days because it has a legal process to follow. Complaints can be made by phone at (918) 684-6235 and are kept anonymous.

Could Muskogee property taxes go up because of the court judgments?

Possibly. The city manager's September 1, 2026 letter said the judgments total $29.25 million and could add about $450 a year per $100,000 of valuation if placed on the sinking fund. The decision would come in June 2027 and any increase would start in October 2027 and last three years.

What percent of value is real property assessed at in Oklahoma?

The state constitution sets the assessment ratio between 11 and 13.5 percent of fair cash value, according to the Muskogee County Assessor. The result is multiplied by the millage rate.

When are property taxes due in Muskogee County?

Under the standard Oklahoma schedule described by county treasurers, at least half is due by December 31 and the second half by March 31. Call the county treasurer at (918) 682-0811 to confirm a current balance.

Can I sell a Muskogee house that has a code violation?

Yes, many buyers will purchase a house with open violations, but the notice may need to be resolved or disclosed at closing. Ask the city for the status and get any cash offer in writing.

Where is Bixby and how is the city laid out?

Alexander Posey, a member of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, settled the area in the late 1800s, and the town took its name from Tams Bixby, a chairman of the Dawes Commission. That patchwork shows today: older homes near the original streets, newer subdivisions spread across the former farmland. A seller should know which part of town the house is in, because river-side and creek-side lots raise different buyer questions than hilltop or interior ones.

What is Bixby's farming heritage, and does it still matter?

Bixby calls itself The Garden Spot of Oklahoma, a nickname it received in 1941 when the town was a regional shipping point for produce. Farmers first grew cotton, wheat and alfalfa in the river bottom, then switched to truck farming of vegetables in the 1930s.

Most of those truck farms later became sod fields, typically Bermuda grass, or were developed for homes and businesses. Only a small share of residents now work in agriculture, but the city still holds its Green Corn Festival each June.

Gas deposits discovered in 1905 and 1906 and oil fields in 1913 also touched the local economy. For sellers, the useful takeaway is that much of today's housing sits on former farm and river-bottom ground, so soil movement, grading and drainage are fair inspection topics.

What flood and drainage issues come up in Bixby?

Flooding along the Arkansas River and its creeks has been a real planning issue. The city's August 2020 Beacon newsletter said the Haikey Creek levee would bring 920 acres out of the floodplain, addressing one of the last major flood-impaired areas north of the river.

The Oklahoma Water Resources Board lists a floodplain administrator for Bixby, and Oklahoma senators have publicly pushed for funding to repair Arkansas River levee systems that were described as at high risk of failure. A buyer's lender may require flood insurance depending on the map, so check the current flood zone before you set a price.

Practical steps for a seller:

  • Look up the parcel's flood zone before you list.
  • Gather any elevation certificate or past flood insurance claims.
  • Be ready to answer drainage questions about the lot, not only the house.

Who provides utilities and city services in Bixby?

The City of Bixby's Public Works Authority is the local water supplier, and the water itself comes from the City of Tulsa through connections on all sides of town. Bixby's utility service guide also lists providers for sewer, natural gas, telecommunications, electricity and trash, and notes that trash service reaches residents north and south of the river and nearby communities such as Leonard and Liberty.

Bixby Telephone Company, known as BTC Broadband, has offered internet service since 1993 and has installed fiber in select neighborhoods. Confirm which providers serve the specific address, since the city's guide indicates availability can differ north and south of the Arkansas River.

If you are moving out, schedule a final water reading and transfer or stop service on the closing date so the buyer does not inherit your charges.

What do Bixby's code enforcement and permit rules mean for a seller?

Bixby handles code enforcement through its police department, and the city's page explains what does and does not count as a nuisance. For example, a single blade of grass taller than 12 inches is not a violation; the tall growth must cover the majority of the yard as estimated by code enforcement.

Homeowners association covenants are a separate matter from city code. A buyer's agent will often ask about HOA dues and restrictions, so collect your HOA documents early.

The city's Development Services department runs the building permit process and requires electrical, plumbing and mechanical work to be done by contractors licensed with the city, according to its construction guidelines. If you finished a basement, built a deck or replaced a water heater, locate the permit and final inspection records. A cash buyer will usually take a house as is, but missing paperwork is easier to resolve before you sign.

How are Bixby property taxes assessed in Tulsa County?

Most of Bixby is assessed by the Tulsa County Assessor, which values property as of January 1 each year. The assessor's own FAQ explains that assessed value is currently 11 percent of the taxable fair cash value.

Taxable value for homesteads cannot rise more than 3 percent a year, and for other real property the cap is 5 percent. Those caps lift when title transfers, so the buyer's first tax bill can be higher than yours. That is a regular surprise for buyers who rely on the seller's number.

A valuation notice gives you 30 calendar days to file a written protest. The Bixby part in Wagoner County is handled by that county's offices instead.

What is the legal side of a Bixby sale in Oklahoma?

Under 68 O.S. section 3201, the state taxes a conveyed deed at 75 cents per $500 of price. On a $275,000 sale that means 550 units and $412.50, paid through the county clerk at recording.

Oklahoma also requires one- and two-unit sellers to hand the buyer either a condition disclosure or a disclaimer statement, as set out in 60 O.S. section 833 and the Real Estate Commission's forms. Whichever you choose, deliver it in writing.

Bixby Public Schools serves the town. Buyers with children often ask about attendance zones, and part of Broken Arrow also falls in the Bixby district, so confirm the exact boundary for your address.

More questions about Bixby, OK

Is Bixby in Tulsa County or Wagoner County?

Both. The city lies in Tulsa and Wagoner counties. Check your parcel on your tax notice to see which assessor and clerk apply.

Can I sell my Bixby house if it is in a floodplain?

Yes. Flood zone status affects insurance and lending for a conventional buyer, which is why a cash sale can be simpler. Look up the parcel's current flood zone before discussing price.

What does the Bixby code enforcement office look for?

Its page describes violations such as overgrown yards that cover most of the lot, and explains that one tall blade of grass is not a violation. Check the city's code page for the full list.

Who pays Oklahoma documentary stamps when a house is sold?

The statute reaches anyone who signs or sells the deed, and the Tax Commission says both parties can be held responsible. Your contract states who pays at closing.

How soon can I protest a Tulsa County valuation?

You have 30 calendar days from the date on the Notice of Valuation to file a written protest with the Tulsa County Assessor. Call (918) 596-5100 for help.

Where is Shawnee, Oklahoma, and how big is it?

Shawnee is the county seat of Pottawatomie County, in central Oklahoma, just under 40 miles east of downtown Oklahoma City along Interstate 40. The Census Bureau counted 31,377 residents in 2020, and Wikipedia lists the city as the principal city of the Shawnee Micropolitan Statistical Area and part of the Oklahoma City-Shawnee Combined Statistical Area.

The city covers about 41 square miles of land and water combined, at an elevation of roughly 1,053 feet. The median age in 2020 was 35.5, and 16.7 percent of residents were 65 or older.

One housing detail from the 2020 census stands out for sellers. Shawnee had 13,650 housing units but 11,980 households, a gap of about 1,670 units. That does not tell you how any single house will sell, but it does mean buyers here have more choice than the population figure alone suggests.

How did Shawnee begin?

Shawnee was founded on July 4, 1895, after a land run in 1891 opened surplus land belonging to the Sac and Fox, Citizen Potawatomi and Shawnee peoples. The claims of Etta B. Ray and three other settlers became the townsite, and the city was named for the tribe that had lived there.

Railroads built the town. The Choctaw, Oklahoma and Gulf Railroad ran through the claim, and the Santa Fe and the Missouri, Kansas and Texas followed in 1903 and 1904. By 1902 the area had seven cotton gins and two compresses, and 150,000 bales of cotton shipped out in a single year, according to Wikipedia. Shawnee even had electric streetcars from 1904 until 1927.

Oklahoma Baptist University opened in 1910, and the old St. Gregory's campus became the OBU Green Campus after a 2018 sale and 2019 donation.

How do tornadoes and storms affect selling a Shawnee house?

Shawnee has taken direct tornado hits in recent memory, and buyers and insurers know it. An EF4 tornado struck on May 19, 2013, and killed two people. In 2023 two high-end EF2 tornadoes crossed the area in the first four months of the year, on February 26 and April 19. The April storm hit Shawnee directly and damaged the high school and the OBU campus.

For a seller this means a few practical things:

  • Keep roof, window and siding repair records, and any insurance claim paperwork, in one folder.
  • Say plainly whether storm damage has been fully repaired, partly repaired or left alone.
  • If the house has a storm shelter or safe room, document when it was installed and who built it.

Shawnee Public Schools' own district page lists secure entrances, safe rooms and storm shelters at its schools and has a Storm Recovery page. A buyer is likely to ask about it. A direct answer on your house builds trust faster than a vague one.

Which school districts serve Shawnee addresses?

Most of the city is in Shawnee Public Schools, which calls itself the largest and most comprehensive district in Pottawatomie County and says it was founded in 1895. It teaches preschool through 12th grade, with programs in areas such as aviation, cybersecurity, robotics and STEM.

Not every Shawnee address is in that district, though. Wikipedia lists other districts that cover parts of the city:

  • North Rock Creek Public School
  • Bethel Public Schools
  • Dale Public Schools
  • McLoud Public Schools
  • South Rock Creek, Pleasant Grove and Grove (elementary)

If a buyer asks about schools, check the district boundary for the exact address before you answer. A house on the edge of the city can sit in a different district from the one across the street.

The vacant-building form lists temporary exemptions, which can be approved on written request, for disaster-affected properties, structures under construction, properties listed with a licensed Oklahoma realtor and vacant properties being marketed for rent.

Reports and questions go to the city's Action Center at 405-878-1602. If you have inherited a house you do not plan to keep, an open violation does not stop you from selling it, but it does shape what a buyer will pay and how fast you can close.

Who handles property tax for Shawnee homes?

Pottawatomie County. The County Assessor values the property, and the County Treasurer collects the tax. In 2026 the Assessor reported mailing valuation notices on April 6, with an informal appeal or reinspection request due by May 5.

Oklahoma law, in 68 O.S. section 2892, says a homestead application may be filed at any time, but it counts for the current year only if filed by March 15 or within 30 days of a valuation-increase notice. If you are selling, check that your homestead exemption is in place for the year of sale, since it affects the bill the title company prorates.

The Treasurer's office is at 309 North Broadway Avenue in Shawnee, open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. You can pay online, or mail a payment to P.O. Box 3069, Shawnee, OK 74802. The county's page does not list due dates, so ask the office at 405-273-0213 for the current schedule rather than assuming it matches another county.

Which colleges and roads matter for Shawnee buyers?

Interstate 40 is the main route, putting Oklahoma City employers within commuting range. Oklahoma Baptist University, which opened in 1910, anchors a campus in town, and Wikipedia notes the St. Gregory's campus was folded into it.

Shawnee's mayor-council government runs the code and permitting side, through the Community Development Office at 405-878-1601. The city's online portal lets residents report issues such as dilapidated or unsecured structures, tall weeds and abandoned vehicles.

If you own a rental near campus or along I-40 and want out, tenants in place are a separate question. Review the lease terms and notice rules before you decide on a sale route, and talk with a local attorney if the situation is complicated.

What are your options for selling a house in Shawnee?

You can list it, sell it yourself, or sell as-is to a cash buyer. Each fits a different situation.

  • List with an agent: best when the house is in good shape and you can wait for showings and a buyer's financing.
  • Sell yourself: saves commission but puts pricing, paperwork and negotiation on you.
  • Cash sale as-is: suits houses with storm damage, deferred repairs, code notices, tenants or probate complications, since the buyer does not need a lender's repair conditions.

Whichever route you choose, gather the deed, any code notices, repair and insurance records, and your latest tax statement first. Those documents make every option faster.

More questions about Shawnee, OK

Is Shawnee in Pottawatomie County?

Yes. Shawnee is the county seat of Pottawatomie County, so the county assessor and treasurer there handle property valuation and tax bills.

Do I have to register a vacant house in Shawnee?

Yes, under Ordinance No. 2818NS vacant properties must register with the city. Temporary exemptions can be approved on written request, including for properties listed with a licensed Oklahoma realtor.

How long does Shawnee code enforcement take to resolve a violation?

The city says nuisance cases such as tall weeds or junk generally resolve in 45 to 60 days, while property maintenance cases can take at least six months from the report.

Can I sell a Shawnee house that has tornado damage?

Yes. You can sell it as is to a cash buyer, or repair it first and list it. Keep photos, insurance paperwork and repair estimates so the buyer sees the damage clearly.

Where do I pay property tax in Shawnee?

Pay the Pottawatomie County Treasurer, online or by mail to P.O. Box 3069, Shawnee, OK 74802. The office is at 309 North Broadway Avenue and can be reached at 405-273-0213.

Where is Jenks, and what sets it apart from the rest of the Tulsa area?

Jenks is a Tulsa County suburb of Tulsa, set between the Arkansas River and U.S. Route 75 in northeastern Oklahoma. The city covers about 18 square miles at an elevation near 617 feet, and the Census Bureau estimate already on this page puts the population at 28,175 for July 2025.

Much of the city's identity comes from the river. The Riverwalk Crossing pedestrian bridge links the Jenks Riverwalk to the South Tulsa River Parks. The Oklahoma Aquarium is in Jenks, and the downtown area carries the nickname Antique Capital of Oklahoma.

For a seller, the practical point is that Jenks sits in the Tulsa metro but has its own city hall, permit office and ordinances, so local rules apply even when a buyer is shopping the whole region.

How did Jenks grow, and why does flood history matter?

Jenks began in 1904 as a community site on the Midland Valley Railroad between Tulsa and Muskogee, and it was named for the railroad's owner and director, William Henry Jenks. The town was platted in July 1905, the same year the Glenn Pool oil discovery brought business people and oil depots to the area.

When oil production slowed, farming took over again. Bulgarian families who immigrated in the 1920s set up vegetable farms. Floods from the Arkansas River and Polecat Creek struck repeatedly from 1904 through the 1950s, and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built a levee around Jenks in 1948. Another severe flood threat arrived in 1986, when releases from Keystone Dam reached up to 300,000 cubic feet per second.

Anyone selling near the river or a creek should expect buyers and lenders to ask about floodplain status. Pull your elevation certificate or flood insurance paperwork if you have it, since it answers the question before it is asked.

Jenks has a mix of manufacturing, utilities, finance and tourism. Kimberly-Clark built a manufacturing facility in the 1980s, and Public Service Company of Oklahoma, Green Country Energy, Tulsa Winch, Continental Wire Cloth and First Oklahoma Bank are listed as companies headquartered or based in the city.

The Richard Lloyd Jones Jr. Airport opened just outside Jenks in 1958 and spurred growth. The Tulsa water system and a gas-fired power plant expanded into Jenks in the 1970s. A citizen-led effort began in 2024 to restore abandoned infrastructure in an area called The Ten District.

  • Population grew from 16,924 in 2010 to 25,949 in 2020, a gain of roughly 9,000 residents in ten years.
  • The river crossing was rebuilt as the town grew: a single-lane bridge in 1910, a two-lane bridge in 1948 and a four-lane bridge in 1996.
  • The current high school building dates to 1960 and 1961.

Which schools serve Jenks addresses?

Jenks Public Schools is the main district, and it received the 2005 Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award. It is one of the largest districts in the state, and many of its schools stand inside the City of Tulsa, so a Jenks school zone does not always mean a Jenks mailing address.

Parts of the area are also served by Bixby Public Schools and Glenpool Public Schools. Confirm the district for a specific address with the school office before you advertise it, so a buyer does not rely on the wrong assumption.

Jenks regulates storm shelters through its permit office. A permit is needed for outdoor storm shelters, in-ground safe rooms and above-ground safe rooms built on site. If you installed a shelter, find the permit and the manufacturer paperwork before you list. A permitted, standards-compliant shelter is a documented feature a buyer can verify. An unpermitted one can raise questions at inspection.

Permit applications are picked up at City Hall, second floor, 211 N Elm Street, or printed from the city's Protective Inspections page, and the city says processing takes at least three working days.

How are Tulsa County property taxes handled when a Jenks house sells?

The Tulsa County Assessor values property as of January 1 each year and mails a notice whenever the fair cash value increases. A taxpayer then has 30 calendar days from the date of the notice to protest in writing, or can protest by the first Monday in April even without an increase.

The Treasurer says at least half of the tax must be paid before January 1, and the second half before April 1. If half is not paid before January 1, the whole amount becomes due and is treated as delinquent.

One detail matters to your buyer. The assessor states that when a home is purchased, the statutory cap on its taxable value is removed, and properties are revalued every year. A buyer's tax bill can therefore differ from yours, which is worth saying early if the buyer is budgeting. Start with paperwork, then condition. Gather the tax statement, any floodplain or shelter permits, and the Oklahoma disclosure form. State law requires a seller to deliver a disclaimer or disclosure statement before the buyer's offer is accepted, and a buyer may sue if it is missing. The statute is 60 O.S. section 833 and the sections near it.

Then decide how fast you need to move. A listing can bring a financed buyer, but it comes with showings, inspections and a buyer's lender timeline. A direct cash sale shortens the path and takes the house in the condition it is in. If the property sits in a mapped flood area, has an unpermitted addition or has unpaid tax, tell us up front so the offer reflects the real situation.

Our editorial team writes these guides to explain choices, and any offer for a Jenks house is for you to accept or decline.

No. Jenks is its own city in Tulsa County and a suburb of Tulsa. Many Jenks school buildings are physically inside Tulsa, which is why the school district and the mailing city can differ.

Yes for outdoor shelters, in-ground safe rooms and on-site built above-ground safe rooms. Prefabricated above-ground safe rooms do not need one. The shelter must meet FEMA P-320 or ICC-500 and the city says processing takes at least three working days.

Does Jenks have flood risk?

The city has a floodplain development permit process, and local history includes repeated floods before a levee was built in 1948 and a flood threat in 1986. Check the floodplain status of your parcel with the city engineering office at 918-299-5883.

What happens to my property tax cap when I sell a Jenks home?

The Tulsa County Assessor says the cap on taxable value is removed when a home is purchased. The buyer's first bill can be higher than yours, so share your tax statement but tell the buyer to confirm with the assessor.

When are Tulsa County taxes due?

At least half before January 1 and the second half before April 1, according to the County Treasurer. Missing the first-half deadline makes the full amount due and subject to delinquent tax rules.
